6082: Contemporary evangelical historian whose books correct common misunderstandings of Arminianism, arguing that classical Arminianism is a theology of grace rooted in the Reformation, not semi-Pelagianism.
6083: Arminianism arose inside the Dutch Reformed church. After Arminius's death his followers presented the Five Articles of the Remonstrance (1610) to the States of Holland, arguing for conditional election, universal atonement, the necessity of grace, resistible grace and an open question about perseverance. The national Synod of Dort (1618–1619) condemned them, and Remonstrant ministers were deposed; the political turmoil included the execution of the statesman Oldenbarnevelt. Arminian ideas found later homes in the Church of England (the 'Laudian' party), among the General Baptists, and above all in Wesleyan Methodism, whose missionary success made Arminian soteriology dominant in much of global evangelicalism, Pentecostalism and the Holiness movement.

6152:
Molinism holds that God possesses 'middle knowledge': knowledge, logically prior to his decision to create, of what every possible free creature would freely do in every possible set of circumstances. Using this knowledge God chooses to actualise a world in which his purposes are infallibly achieved through, not in spite of, genuinely (libertarian) free choices.

Applied to salvation, God's election is his choice to create a world in which particular people freely respond to his grace; predestination is real and specific, yet nobody is determined to believe or to reject. Molinists argue this combines a strong doctrine of providence with a strong doctrine of human freedom and God's universal salvific will.
6154: Spanish Jesuit theologian, professor at Évora
6155: Jesuit who developed the theory of scientia media (middle knowledge) to reconcile grace, foreknowledge, providence and free will. His *Concordia* sparked a long and bitter dispute with Dominican Thomists (notably Domingo Báñez), leading to the papal Congregatio de Auxiliis, which ended in 1607 without condemning either side.
6158: Analytic philosopher of religion (Calvin College, Notre Dame)

6163: Catholic philosopher whose book is the standard systematic statement of the Molinist account of providence in contemporary philosophy.
6167: Evangelical apologist who has done more than anyone to introduce Molinism to Protestant audiences, applying it to providence, the problem of evil, biblical prophecy and the question of those who never hear the gospel.
6170: Baptist theologian, Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary
6171: Keathley applied Molinism directly to soteriology, replacing TULIP with the acronym ROSES (Radical depravity, Overcoming grace, Sovereign election, Eternal life, Singular redemption) and arguing that grace is 'overcoming' though resistible because God's grace works until a person refuses.
6172: Molinism emerged in Counter-Reformation Catholicism during the De Auxiliis controversy between Jesuits and Dominicans over how efficacious grace relates to free will, a Catholic parallel to the Protestant debates that culminated at Dort. Arminius may have read Molina and used similar ideas, though how much is debated. After centuries of relative neglect in Protestantism, Molinism was revived in analytic philosophy of religion in the 1970s (Plantinga) and popularised among evangelicals by W. L. Craig. It is attractive to some Baptists and others who want a high view of providence without Calvinist determinism.
6173: 1. God has three logical moments of knowledge: natural knowledge (all possibilities), middle knowledge (what free creatures would do in any circumstances), and free knowledge (what will actually happen, given his decree).
6174: 2. Human beings have libertarian freedom with respect to responding to grace; no prior condition determines whether they will believe.
6175: 3. God chose to create a world, among those feasible given creaturely freedom, in which his purposes, including the salvation of particular people, are accomplished.
6176: 4. Election is therefore specific and certain, yet not causally determining: the elect freely believe, and the lost freely reject grace sufficient for salvation.
6177: 5. Christ died for all and God sincerely desires the salvation of all; God may arrange circumstances so that the maximum number of people freely respond.
6178: 6. God is the author of the world's providential order but not of sin, because he does not cause free choices, he only permits them knowing what they will be.
6179: God tells David that Saul would come and the men of Keilah would surrender him if he stayed; David leaves and neither happens. God knows true conditionals about what free agents would do.
6180: Jesus says Tyre, Sidon and Sodom would have repented if they had seen his works: knowledge of counterfactuals about free human responses.
6181: Christ was delivered up by God’s definite plan and foreknowledge, yet killed by lawless hands: providence working through free, culpable acts.
6182: Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and Israel did what God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place, illustrating sovereign planning that does not cancel culpability.
6183: God determined the times and places of peoples so that they would seek him: providential arrangement of circumstances with a view to free response.
6184: Had the rulers understood, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory: another true counterfactual of freedom woven into God’s plan.
6185: A person plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps: human planning and divine direction both real.
6186: God desires all to be saved; middle knowledge lets God pursue this desire within the constraints of what free creatures would do.
6187: Scripture attributes to God knowledge of what free creatures would do in circumstances that never occur, which is precisely middle knowledge.
6188: Middle knowledge allows God to exercise meticulous providence without causally determining choices, so he can be sovereign without being the author of sin.
6189: It explains how God can both truly desire everyone's salvation and specifically elect those who will be saved: God chooses among feasible worlds, perhaps one with an optimal balance of saved and lost.
6190: Texts that join divine determination with human guilt, such as the crucifixion narratives, are best explained by a God who decrees through foreseen free acts.
6191: Simple foreknowledge does not help God plan; middle knowledge does, giving the Arminian concern for freedom a robust account of providence.
6192: Molina's view received an extended hearing in the Catholic Church and was never condemned (Congregatio de Auxiliis, ended 1607), and it independently resurfaced in Plantinga's free will defence, suggesting conceptual power.
6193: The grounding objection: what makes counterfactuals of libertarian freedom true before the person exists or decides? If nothing grounds them, they cannot be known. (Raised by Robert Adams and William Hasker, among others.)
6194: Molinism does not avoid the hard questions it accuses Calvinism of: God still knowingly creates a world in which specific people will be lost, and chooses not to create a world in which they would have been saved.
6195: Some Arminians (e.g. Roger Olson) worry that Molinism collapses into a form of determinism: if God selects the world precisely to produce particular choices, the creature's freedom seems a mere instrument in a deterministic plan.
6196: Molinism is a philosophical theory imported to resolve an exegetical debate. Scripture nowhere describes a logical sequence of divine knowledges, and ordinary believers should not need speculative metaphysics to understand salvation.
6197: Lutheran theology warns against speculating about the hidden God (Deus absconditus) and directs faith to God revealed in Christ; Molinism tries to explain what Luther and the Formula of Concord deliberately leave as mystery.
6198: Orthodox theologians see Molinism as a product of Western scholasticism that treats God's knowledge in rationalistic, quasi-temporal stages and focuses on decrees rather than on communion and participation in God.
6199: The proof-texts do not establish middle knowledge: 1 Sam 23 can be read as God's knowledge of Saul's and the Keilahites' settled intentions, and Matt 11:21 as hyperbole; neither need involve libertarian freedom.
6200: Molinists reply that counterfactuals need not be grounded in a causal sense any more than future-tense statements need be; it suffices that the person would in fact choose that way. They also argue that the grounding demand, applied strictly, would undermine knowledge of the future or the past too.
6201: Molinists accept that God's choice of world is sovereign and inscrutable, but stress the difference: in Molinism those lost freely reject sufficient grace and would do so in any feasible world (transworld damnation is one proposal, Craig), whereas in Calvinism God withholds the grace that would have saved them.
6202: Molinists reply that God's selecting a world does not cause the choices within it; it is the counterfactual truths themselves, which God does not control, that make the outcome what it is. That is exactly the difference from determinism.
6203: Molinists grant that middle knowledge is a model, not a doctrine stated in Scripture, but argue that every view involves models (compatibilism, foreknowledge) and that Molinism is constrained by texts like 1 Sam 23 and Matt 11 that require counterfactual knowledge.

6208: Molinists hold God's middle knowledge is innate and eternal, not learned from observation; God's knowledge is not caused by creatures.

6223:
Provisionism holds that God has made a genuine provision of salvation for every person in Christ's death and that the gospel, empowered by the Holy Spirit, is itself sufficient to enable any hearer to respond in faith. Unlike Calvinism it denies that fallen people are totally unable to believe the gospel, and unlike classical Arminianism it does not posit a separate inward prevenient grace: the Spirit-inspired word is the means of enabling.

Election is understood corporately (God chose to save those in Christ, and chose Israel and the apostles for service), and believers are eternally secure. Proponents see their view as the plain reading of Scripture and as the historic conviction of most non-Calvinist Baptists.

6227: Helwys led the first Baptist congregation in England (Spitalfields, 1612) and wrote an early plea for religious liberty. They are historical forerunners of non-Calvinist Baptist soteriology, though their theology was broadly Arminian and differed from modern provisionism on points such as perseverance.
